doc.title: Chico Freeman interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001

title: Originality of the greats: Armstrong, Lester Young, Mal Waldron
summary: He argues that all the major figures were original, citing Mal Waldron's advice and the Lester Young versus Hawkins story.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: No I think the record companies encourage musicians who sound like other musicians, musicians who are going back ten, twenty, thirty years, and trying to play like the people who invented and created that music at that time and sort of regurgitated, you know, almost like a repertory concept. And as opposed to the industry encouraging and signing and promoting original thinking musicians and artists to try to take the music further. You know we’ve always looked forward. You think of the greats, let’s talk about the greats, the major exponents of the music that we all have come to admire and hold up as the defining factors. Right? You look at people like Monk, Charlie Parker, Duke Ellington, Count Basie, Louis Armstrong, Billie Holiday. When you look at these people, they have one thing in common and that is they were all original. Louis Armstrong was doing nothing that anybody else was doing. In fact, Mal Waldron, I work with Mal Waldon and Mal Waldron told me once that a musician would come and hear a guy play and if he was doing something that the musician had been doing for himself he would probably stop doing that to try to do something different. The originality was a very important thing. You listen to the sound between a Coleman Hawkins and a Lester Young or Ben Webster and Lester Young, you can hear that Lester Young was completely about being his own man. You know that story about in the band, I think it was Fletcher Henderson’s wife or somebody’s wife—
I know, we don’t want to misquote.
They had to replace Coleman Hawkins.

Yes, and they took Lester Young down in the basement and played all these records of Coleman Hawkins and asked him — and Lester replied, “If you want him then you hire him.” So you know Thelonious Monk, his style, and you look at all the great — McCoy Tyner, Thelonious Monk, Bud Powell, you know as far as pianists go. Bill Evans. You know you listen to these pianists. Wynton Kelly. Red Garland. They sound different.
They have their own sounds. Andrew Hill. Saxophone players — from Chu Berry to Lester Young to Coleman Hawkins to Ben Webster, Ornette Coleman, Charlie Parker, Eric Dolphy.
